title: How long did you really work?
bodyMd:
Ask a hundred employed adults how many hours they worked last week and the average will come out well above the figure in their employers' records. The gap is not usually dishonesty. Asked to summarise a week, people reach for the hours they were expected to work, add the evenings they remember as difficult, and forget the slow Tuesday when the office emptied early. The answer is a portrait of how the week felt, not a measurement of how it went.

Researchers who want a measurement use a time diary instead. Participants record, for one or two assigned days, what they were doing in each ten-minute interval, ideally on the same day or the morning after. When diaries are set beside questionnaires answered by the same people, they generally report fewer hours of paid work (for the heaviest workers, sometimes several hours fewer a week) and more hours of sleep and of unplanned time. Diaries also reveal something questionnaires cannot: which activities were carried out at the same time. A parent who is cooking, listening to a child read and answering a message appears in a questionnaire as three separate jobs and in a diary as one hour in which each was done imperfectly.

None of this makes diaries the last word. They are burdensome, so the people who volunteer to keep them tend to be those with a little spare time, and a single day says little about someone whose schedule changes from week to week. A survey office therefore faces a trade-off between depth and coverage: it can ask a few people to say a great deal, or many people to say very little. Public debate about whether the working week is getting longer has often ignored that choice, comparing a figure from one kind of instrument with a figure from the other as if they were interchangeable.

The practical lesson is modest. Before treating a statistic about time as a fact about behaviour, it is worth asking how the hours were collected. The same society can look overworked in one survey and comparatively relaxed in another without anyone having changed how they live.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph social-science passage of about 355 words titled "How long did you really work?". The first paragraph says that people asked how many hours they worked last week report more than their employers' records show, not out of dishonesty but because a summary of a week reflects how it felt rather than how it went. The second paragraph describes time diaries, in which participants record what they did in each ten-minute interval on assigned days; compared with questionnaires from the same people, diaries generally report fewer hours of paid work and more sleep and unplanned time, and they reveal which activities happened at the same time, illustrated by a parent cooking, listening to a child read and answering a message. The third paragraph gives limits of diaries: they are burdensome so volunteers tend to have spare time, one day says little about variable schedules, and survey offices face a trade-off between depth and coverage; public debate often compares figures from the two kinds of instrument as if interchangeable. The fourth paragraph concludes that one should ask how hours were collected before treating a statistic about time as a fact about behaviour.
